title: Constant sized support state distillation with qubit recycling
abstract: In order to circumvent that no universal set of gates can be achieved on a given quantum error-correcting codes, additional gates can be performed through magic state injection. This however requires to have access to high fidelity magic state, which can be obtained by the distillation of low quality states to fewer higher quality ones. In this paper, we provide a family of distillation protocols able to produce diagonal states at every level of the Clifford hierarchy. This family is obtained recursively using code doubling techniques and leveraging qubit recycling, the fact that some idle qubits of the protocols can be measured and re-used. At a given level of the Clifford hierarchy, we show that the protocols we derive can be performed at arbitrary high distance on a fix number of logical qubits. This family recovers many known efficient protocols, and uncovers new ones, such as a $111 \to 1$ protocol for $|T\rangle$ state distillation at distance $7$, which are the most compact in term of volume. Finally, we discuss possible extension of this framework for distillation protocols producing more than one output state.
summary: This paper develops a systematic, recursive framework for designing quantum state distillation protocols necessary for fault-tolerant quantum computation. By utilizing code doubling and qubit recycling techniques, the authors construct families of protocols that achieve high code distance with minimal resource overhead. This work advances the theoretical understanding of resource management in quantum error correction.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitation that quantum error-correcting codes alone cannot provide a universal set of fault-tolerant logical gates, necessitating high-fidelity magic state injection.
main_result: The authors provide a recursive family of distillation protocols that can produce diagonal states at arbitrary high distance on a fixed number of logical qubits, significantly reducing resource overhead via qubit recycling.
method: The core method involves constructing and analyzing families of weakly r-orthogonal matrices using code doubling techniques and algebraic proofs over F_2.
model_or_system: The model is based on quantum error-correcting codes and the distillation of magic states (like the |T> state). The mathematical framework uses r-orthogonal matrices G to characterize the resource requirements.
key_observables: Distance (d), Support (s), Depth (n), and the minimal recycled qubit support (s*).
important_parameters: The orthogonality level r, the distance d, and the number of output states k.
main_assumptions: The analysis primarily focuses on Z-type errors sufficient for stabilizer codes, and the construction relies on the availability of lower-level Clifford operations.
figures_summary: The notes mention a Table I comparing parameters (s, s*, n, d, effective overhead) of the constructed G(r,d) protocols against known literature protocols.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first defining the problem using r-orthogonal matrices, then introducing the code-doubling construction (Theorem 1), establishing a recursive family construction, and finally proving the properties (orthogonality, distance, support bounds) of the resulting matrices.
why_interesting: The focus on resource optimization (qubit recycling) and achieving high-distance distillation protocols is highly relevant for scaling up quantum computation architectures.
